intro: Density clustering begins with local neighborhoods. Whether a point is a core point depends on how many observations lie within a fixed radius.
task: Return the inclusive radius-neighbor matrix and a boolean vector identifying core observations.
requirements: points is an (n,d) matrix. radius is a scalar in [0,1e6] and min_points is an integer in [1,n].
neighbors[i,j] is true exactly when Euclidean distance is <=radius. Include each observation itself and include duplicate observations separately.
Return {"neighbors": boolean (n,n) matrix, "core": boolean (n,) vector} using neighbor_count>=min_points. This step does not assign DBSCAN cluster labels.

Use real finite numeric inputs with magnitude at most 1e6, excluding booleans. Vectors have length 1..128 and matrix axes have length 1..128 unless a tighter bound is stated. Leave all inputs unchanged; raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Find the structure
hints.body: Broadcast point differences to build all pair distances, then threshold them into a boolean matrix.

hints.title: Build the calculation
hints.body: The diagonal and duplicate observations contribute to neighborhood counts; include distances exactly at the radius.

explanation: The neighbor matrix represents local density using an inclusive distance threshold. Counting the diagonal follows the convention that an observation belongs to its own neighborhood.
Core membership is only one stage of density clustering. Border and noise classification also require connectivity through core points and should not be inferred from this boolean vector alone.
